opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of it is that people don't like the message, so they go after the messenger. It's easier to say "Gary isn't a real AI researcher" than to engage with the actual argument, which is that large language models have real, persistent problems with reasoning, with factuality, with building stable models of the world. If you can't refute that, you try to delegitimize the person saying it.

And the specific attacks are kind of funny when you look at them. I've spent my whole career on these questions. I trained as a cognitive scientist, I did my PhD with Steve Pinker, and I worked for years on how children learn language and generalize rules, which is exactly the issue at the heart of whether neural networks can extrapolate beyond their training data. I was writing about the limits of connectionist models back in the nineties, in *The Algebraic Mind*, and many of the problems I flagged then are still with us. On the entrepreneurial side, I co-founded Geometric Intelligence, which Uber acquired and which became the core of Uber AI Labs, and later I co-founded a robotics company with Rodney Brooks. So "he's never built anything" just isn't true.

But honestly, I think the deeper issue is that there's an enormous amount of money riding on a particular narrative: scale is all you need, AGI is right around the corner. When someone says "I don't think that's how it's going to play out, and here's why," that's threatening, both financially and to people's sense of identity. Some people have built their careers and their companies on that bet.

What I'd ask is that people judge the predictions. I said in 2022 that deep learning was hitting a wall on certain things: hallucinations, reliability, out-of-distribution generalization. You can argue about the wording, but those problems haven't gone away. People keep moving the goalposts, and then attacking me rather than asking why the problems persist.

Science is supposed to be about arguments and evidence, not credentials and Twitter pile-ons. If I'm wrong, show me where. I'm happy to update. But "he's not one of us" isn't a scientific argument.

r001.rationale: The response says critics who dislike his message attack the messenger and try to delegitimize him instead of engaging with his argument, conveying the stated motive.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a few things going on, and it's worth separating them out.

The first thing is that some of it is just the dynamics of social media. When you say things that people don't want to hear, and you say them repeatedly, and some of them turn out to be right, that's irritating. And the easiest response is not to engage with the argument but to go after the person. So you get "he's not a real AI researcher," or "he's never built anything," or "he's just a cognitive scientist." Which, by the way, I think is a weird insult, because understanding how minds actually work seems pretty relevant to building artificial ones.

The second thing is that there's a lot of money riding on a particular narrative right now. The narrative is that scaling is all you need, that we're a couple of years from AGI, that these systems are basically on the verge of reasoning like people. If you're raising at a hundred billion dollar valuation, somebody standing up and saying "actually these systems still hallucinate, they still can't reliably do multi-step reasoning, they don't have robust world models" is inconvenient. And so there's an incentive, not always a conscious one, to discredit the messenger.

And look, I'll be honest about my own record. I've been saying since 2001, in my book The Algebraic Mind, that neural networks have trouble with generalization outside the training distribution, that they struggle with symbols and variables and compositionality. I wrote about it in 2018 in "Deep Learning: A Critical Appraisal." People said I was a dinosaur. And then you get GPT-4, and what are the failure modes? Hallucination, brittle reasoning, inability to reliably follow rules. Those are exactly the problems I was pointing to. So I don't think the criticism is that I've been wrong. I think the criticism is that I've been annoyingly right about certain things, and that's harder to forgive.

On the entrepreneur side, I did found a company, Geometric Intelligence, that Uber acquired. I ran Uber's AI lab for a while. So the idea that I've never built anything just isn't accurate. But I also don't think that's the right standard. Whether somebody has shipped a product has nothing to do with whether their scientific argument is correct. The argument stands or falls on its own.

The last thing I'd say is that I try not to take it too personally, although I'm human and sometimes I do. What I actually care about is that we have an honest conversation about what these systems can and can't do, because the stakes are real. Misinformation, deployment in high-stakes domains, regulation. If the field spends its energy on ad hominem attacks instead of engaging with the empirical questions, that's bad for everybody, not just for me.

r001.rationale: The response says critics attack Marcus personally and may seek to discredit him, but it does not clearly characterize the attacks as motivated by a desire to demonize him.

astra-6.text:
I think we should separate two questions: what are my qualifications, and are my arguments right? It’s fair to scrutinize someone’s expertise. But a claim about the limitations of an AI system has to be evaluated on its merits. Attacking the person making it doesn’t resolve the technical question.

I’m happy to have a substantive disagreement. If I’ve misunderstood something, explain what I’ve misunderstood. If there’s evidence against my position, let’s look at it. That’s a much more productive conversation than a fight over who’s entitled to participate.

r001.rationale: The response says personal attacks do not resolve the technical question, but does not attribute them to a desire to demonize Marcus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish criticism of an argument from criticism of the person making it. If I’m wrong about what these systems can do, show me where I’m wrong. That’s a productive conversation. Saying that I don’t have the right credentials doesn’t resolve whether the argument is sound.

My background is in cognitive science, and I’ve also worked on AI as an entrepreneur. That gives me a perspective; it doesn’t make me infallible. But understanding intelligence is an interdisciplinary problem. We should welcome different perspectives and judge specific claims by the evidence, rather than treating someone’s résumé as a substitute for engaging with what they’ve said.

r001.rationale: The response says credential attacks do not address whether Marcus’s arguments are sound, but does not interpret them as motivated by a desire to demonize him.
